analysis.one_liner: Caps what families pay for phone calls from prison and bans carrier commissions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from December 2005 until the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Phone calls from prison are among the most expensive calls in America — some reaching $1 a minute plus a $3.95 connection fee — and they are usually paid by the family member receiving the call, often a low-income household. The bill would have directed the FCC to cap per-minute and per-call charges, require carriers to offer cheaper debit-account calling alongside collect calls, ban the commissions carriers pay prisons for the exclusive right to provide service, and require prisons to allow more than one phone provider so families could choose a cheaper option.
analysis.who_benefits: Families of incarcerated people, who typically pay for the calls and are disproportionately low-income. The bill's findings note that high call rates weaken family ties that research links to lower recidivism and successful reentry after prison.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families paying for calls from prison

how_it_helps.text: The FCC would have to consider setting a maximum uniform per-minute rate and a maximum per-call connection rate for calls from correctional institutions, where some rates reach $1 per minute plus $3.95 per call.

Providers would have to offer both collect calling and cheaper prepaid debit-account options, and prisons would have to allow more than one carrier so prisoners and their families could choose the lowest-rate provider.

The bill would prohibit carriers from paying commissions to prison administrators for exclusive rights to provide inmate phone service — payments that in some cases account for 50 percent or more of total charges and are passed on to families.
The bill states that excessive rates burden family contact, which studies link to lower recidivism, successful reentry, and reduced future imprisonment costs.

analysis.who_pays: Prison telephone carriers, whose exclusive contracts and commission payments would be regulated away, and state correctional departments, which would lose commission revenue they currently collect from inmate call charges.
analysis.who_pays_short: Prison phone carriers and corrections agencies

drawbacks.text: The bill would preempt state rules on interstate inmate phone rates and commissions, overriding any stricter state protections already in place.

The FCC would have to write rate rules within a year, and carriers and prisons would lose commission revenue that some correctional systems use to fund inmate programs — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.
The bill directs the FCC only to 'consider' each type of rate regulation rather than mandating specific caps, so the relief families would actually receive depended on later FCC rulemaking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: families, many low-income, were paying some of the highest phone rates in the country largely because of monopoly contracts and commission kickbacks, while the costs fell on the phone carriers and corrections agencies collecting those fees. The bill's main design weakness is that it told the FCC to consider remedies rather than setting the caps itself, and it preempts state rules — but the direction of the benefit, from families to a small number of entrenched carriers, is clear.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Telecommunications Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on December 7, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On December 16, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet, where no further action followed.
Five Democratic colleagues cosponsored the bill; no further committee or floor action appears in the record before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The prison phone industry kept its exclusive contracts and commission arrangements, and state correctional agencies kept collecting commissions — while families continued paying the high per-minute and per-call rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Prison phone carriers and corrections agencies

for.name: Rep. Bobby L. Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote findings documenting that families paid rates as high as $1 per minute plus $3.95 per call, driven by carrier commissions to prisons and the lack of competition.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Telecommunications and Internet Subcommittee and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, and the record shows no vote and no recorded opponents, so the partisan shape of the outcome cannot be measured directly.

industries.note: These carriers held exclusive contracts inside prisons, charged some of the highest rates in the country, and paid commissions of up to 50 percent of charges to prisons for the exclusive right to serve them. The bill would have capped their rates, banned the commissions, and forced competition, directly cutting their revenue at the expense of families who pay the bills.

Correctional administrators collect commissions from carriers based on inmate call revenue; the bill would have banned those payments and barred states from requiring them. Their interest in keeping this revenue ran directly against the families paying the rates.
